answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: b. 1961 · then U.S. senator from Illinois, speaking on Super Tuesday night, 5 February 2008
answer.sourceLine: Obama really did say this, in his election-night remarks in Chicago on 5 February 2008 — the transcript is archived at the American Presidency Project. Two caveats: the transcript reads “or if we wait for some other time,” and the memorable half of the line — “we are the ones we’ve been waiting for” — is the poet June Jordan’s, written in 1978.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Remarks following the “Super Tuesday” primaries and caucuses
Barack Obama, then U.S. senator from Illinois and candidate for the Democratic nomination
“we are the ones we have been waiting for” — June Jordan, “Poem for South African Women” (presented at the United Nations, 9 August 1978)

source.excerpt: It will not be resolved on even a Super Duper Tuesday. Change will not come if we wait for some other person or if we wait for some other time. We are the ones we’ve been waiting for. (Cheers, applause.) We are the change that we seek.
trail: 9 August 1978 — June Jordan presents “Poem for South African Women” at the United Nations, commemorating the 40,000 women and children who marched against the “dompass” on that date in 1956. Its closing line, set in italics: we are the ones we have been waiting for (Academy of American Poets ↗).

2006 — Alice Walker titles a book of essays We Are the Ones We Have Been Waiting For (The New Press) and names her source outright: “It was the poet June Jordan who wrote ‘We are the ones we have been waiting for.’ Sweet Honey in the Rock turned those words into a song” (book excerpt ↗).
5 February 2008 — Obama closes his Super Tuesday remarks in Chicago with the passage, Jordan’s sentence at its centre (American Presidency Project transcript ↗).

Still unsettled — Jordan italicised the line like an epigraph, and both John Edwards and Jim Wallis credited it to the activist Lisa Sullivan, so whether Jordan coined it or quoted it remains open (Peter Levine ↗).
source.excerptNote: As transcribed at the American Presidency Project. Note the transcript’s “or if we wait for some other time” — the version that circulates online drops the repeated clause and stops before “We are the change that we seek.”

author.bio: Barack Obama was a first-term U.S. senator from Illinois when he delivered these remarks on the night of Super Tuesday, 5 February 2008; he was elected the 44th president that November and served until 2017. The 2008 campaign’s signature cadences were often borrowed and remixed rather than coined — this line is a clear case, closing on a sentence the poet June Jordan had written thirty years earlier. Obama never claimed to have originated it.

misattribution.heading: What gets credited to whom
misattribution.intro: This is an unusual case: Obama really did say the sentence, on the record, in a speech anyone can read. What’s wrong is narrower — the half of it that people actually remember was written by someone else, and the wording that circulates isn’t quite what he said.

items.scope: “We are the ones we’ve been waiting for”
items.why: Obama spoke it on Super Tuesday 2008 and the internet has credited him with it ever since. The sentence is the closing line of June Jordan’s Poem for South African Women, presented at the United Nations on 9 August 1978 (Academy of American Poets ↗). As Peter Levine puts it, Obama “didn’t coin it and never said he did” (peterlevine.ws ↗).

The transcript reads “Change will not come if we wait for some other person or if we wait for some other time,” and carries on into a third sentence, “We are the change that we seek.” The circulating version compresses the clause and cuts the ending (American Presidency Project ↗).

items.scope: “We are the ones we have been waiting for”
items.why: The line circulates widely as the climax of an ancient Hopi prophecy. Peter Levine searched for support and reported finding “no evidence that the Hopis were using it long ago” (peterlevine.ws ↗). The earliest documented appearance is still Jordan’s 1978 poem.

items.scope: “We are the ones we have been waiting for”
items.why: Walker’s 2006 New Press book made the phrase famous enough to be misread as hers — but she credits Jordan on the page: “It was the poet June Jordan who wrote ‘We are the ones we have been waiting for’” (excerpt ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Obama said it — Chicago, 5 February 2008, and the transcript is public ↗. But the sentence that made it a slogan belongs to June Jordan ↗, and even she may have been quoting: she set the line in italics, like an epigraph, and researchers have never closed the question of where it came from first.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Super Tuesday 2008 did not settle the Democratic race, and Obama’s speech that night had to make an asset of the deadlock. The argument was that no single primary, and no single candidate, was going to do the work — and the line landed as a rebuke to the idea that a saviour was on the way. It is a strange thing for a candidate to say: stop waiting for me.

The sentence he reached for to say it was already thirty years old. June Jordan wrote “we are the ones we have been waiting for” for the women of South Africa, presenting the poem at the United Nations on 9 August 1978 — the twenty-second anniversary of the 1956 march against the pass laws. Alice Walker took it for a book title in 2006. By 2008 it had travelled far enough from its author that most people first heard it in a campaign speech.
detailsBody: Jordan set the line in italics, as its own stanza — the way a writer treats an epigraph rather than a phrase of her own. That has led researchers to wonder whether she was quoting something older. Peter Levine notes that both John Edwards and the activist Jim Wallis credited the line to the late organiser Lisa Sullivan rather than to Jordan, which would push the chain back further still.

The other common origin story — that it is an ancient Hopi prophecy from Oraibi, Arizona — has no documented support. Levine looked and found “no evidence that the Hopis were using it long ago.” The earliest firmly documented appearance remains Jordan’s 1978 poem.
context.pull: It is a strange thing for a candidate to say: stop waiting for me.
